"authors": "Anuradha V Jagtap, Pawan Kumar, Sharad Gupta, N Abharana, S N Jha, D Bhattacharyya, T G Ajithkumar, C P Vinod",

"executive_summary": "This work reports a modified silica-supported bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst (AuFeHS) for the partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol and acetic acid using hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as a green oxidant. The central motivation is that methane is abundant but difficult to convert selectively, because activated C-H bonds tend toward complete oxidation to CO2, and existing catalysts require high temperature and high pressure. The authors address two catalytic challenges: (1) continuous partial oxidation of methane to methanol at atmospheric pressure, and (2) a selectivity switch to acetic acid by co-feeding CO. In a batch reactor at 10 bar, the optimized AuFeHS catalyst (0.46 wt% Fe, 0.23 wt% Au) reached a methanol yield of 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity, one of the highest reported. In a fixed-bed continuous flow reactor at atmospheric pressure, the yield reached 224 mmol/gFe+Au, the best reported value, with steady production over 7 h and a maximum of 157 µmol at 4 h. Co-feeding CO switched the product to acetic acid (648 µmol/gcat within 4 h) with methanol and CO2 as side products. Characterization (ICP-OES, contact angle, XRD, HRTEM, XPS, XANES/EXAFS, in-situ IR, NMR) established that Fe is atomically dispersed and low-valent Fe 3-δ+ sites (709.5 eV) are key for methane and peroxide activation, while Au nanoparticles (1.3-3.0 nm) provide charge donation and CO activation. Isotope (CD4) labeling confirmed the methyl group originates from methane, and nitrogen feed gave no products, ruling out background reactions. The authors attribute the performance to the synergy between Au and Fe, hydrophobic silica (contact angle 118°), and Lewis acid sites. The paper concludes that tuning active Fe species through bimetallic modulation is a promising route toward commercializing methane-to-oxygenates (M2O) technologies under benign conditions.",

summary.title: Atmospheric pressure continuous flow methane oxidation to methanol and acetic acid using H2O2 over Au-Fe catalyst
summary.authors: Anuradha V Jagtap, Pawan Kumar, Sharad Gupta, N Abharana, S N Jha, D Bhattacharyya, T G Ajithkumar, C P Vinod
summary.executive_summary: This work reports a modified silica-supported bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst (AuFeHS) for the partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol and acetic acid using hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as a green oxidant. The central motivation is that methane is abundant but difficult to convert selectively, because activated C-H bonds tend toward complete oxidation to CO2, and existing catalysts require high temperature and high pressure. The authors address two catalytic challenges: (1) continuous partial oxidation of methane to methanol at atmospheric pressure, and (2) a selectivity switch to acetic acid by co-feeding CO. In a batch reactor at 10 bar, the optimized AuFeHS catalyst (0.46 wt% Fe, 0.23 wt% Au) reached a methanol yield of 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity, one of the highest reported. In a fixed-bed continuous flow reactor at atmospheric pressure, the yield reached 224 mmol/gFe+Au, the best reported value, with steady production over 7 h and a maximum of 157 µmol at 4 h. Co-feeding CO switched the product to acetic acid (648 µmol/gcat within 4 h) with methanol and CO2 as side products. Characterization (ICP-OES, contact angle, XRD, HRTEM, XPS, XANES/EXAFS, in-situ IR, NMR) established that Fe is atomically dispersed and low-valent Fe 3-δ+ sites (709.5 eV) are key for methane and peroxide activation, while Au nanoparticles (1.3-3.0 nm) provide charge donation and CO activation. Isotope (CD4) labeling confirmed the methyl group originates from methane, and nitrogen feed gave no products, ruling out background reactions. The authors attribute the performance to the synergy between Au and Fe, hydrophobic silica (contact angle 118°), and Lewis acid sites. The paper concludes that tuning active Fe species through bimetallic modulation is a promising route toward commercializing methane-to-oxygenates (M2O) technologies under benign conditions.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work reports a modified silica-supported bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst (AuFeHS) for the partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol and acetic acid using hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as a green oxidant. The central motivation is that methane is abundant but difficult to convert selectively, because activated C-H bonds tend toward complete oxidation to CO2, and existing catalysts require high temperature and high pressure. The authors address two catalytic challenges: (1) continuous partial oxidation of methane to methanol at atmospheric pressure, and (2) a selectivity switch to acetic acid by co-feeding CO. In a batch reactor at 10 bar, the optimized AuFeHS catalyst (0.46 wt% Fe, 0.23 wt% Au) reached a methanol yield of 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity, one of the highest reported. In a fixed-bed continuous flow reactor at atmospheric pressure, the yield reached 224 mmol/gFe+Au, the best reported value, with steady production over 7 h and a maximum of 157 µmol at 4 h. Co-feeding CO switched the product to acetic acid (648 µmol/gcat within 4 h) with methanol and CO2 as side products. Characterization (ICP-OES, contact angle, XRD, HRTEM, XPS, XANES/EXAFS, in-situ IR, NMR) established that Fe is atomically dispersed and low-valent Fe 3-δ+ sites (709.5 eV) are key for methane and peroxide activation, while Au nanoparticles (1.3-3.0 nm) provide charge donation and CO activation. Isotope (CD4) labeling confirmed the methyl group originates from methane, and nitrogen feed gave no products, ruling out background reactions. The authors attribute the performance to the synergy between Au and Fe, hydrophobic silica (contact angle 118°), and Lewis acid sites. The paper concludes that tuning active Fe species through bimetallic modulation is a promising route toward commercializing methane-to-oxygenates (M2O) technologies under benign conditions.

Research Context
Methane is abundant but difficult to convert selectively because activated C-H bonds tend toward complete oxidation to CO2. Direct partial oxidation of methane to methanol is considered a holy grail problem in catalysis. Existing catalysts suffer from low product yield and high temperature and high-pressure reaction conditions. Most POM-to-methanol reports use molecular oxygen with frugal conversion to methanol. Prior high-pressure H2O2 processes reported low continuous yields at 20 bar.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to achieve continuous partial oxidation of methane to methanol at atmospheric pressure. The study aims to switch selectivity from methanol to acetic acid by co-feeding CO. The hypothesis is that a hydrophobic Au-Fe catalyst with low-valent Fe sites will activate methane and H2O2 at mild conditions. The hypothesis is that Au nanoparticles stabilize low-valent Fe sites and provide CO activation. The predicted outcome is high methanol yield and selectivity under benign conditions.

Methodological Details
The study used a modified deposition precipitation method to disperse Fe onto hydrophobic silica. The catalyst was supported on hydrophobic silica (HS) with low metal loading. The best catalyst had 0.46 wt% Fe and 0.23 wt% Au, confirmed by ICP-OES. The hydrophobicity of silica was confirmed by contact angle analysis with an observed angle of 118. C-H vibration from silica confirmed the hydrophobic functionalization from HS. Powder XRD showed no Au or Fe reflections, confirming fine metal dispersion. HRTEM showed no Fe particle contrast, indicating atomic dispersion of Fe. HRTEM observed small Au nanoparticles of 1.3-3.0 nm in AuFeHS. Elemental mapping showed Au nanoparticles finely dispersed over FeHS. The specific surface area was 392 m2/g for AuFeHS. XPS confirmed Fe3+ at 710.3 eV and FeOOH at 712.5 eV in FeHS. XPS showed low-valent Fe 3-δ+ at 709.5 eV in AuFeHS. XPS estimated 85% Au0 and 15% Auδ+ atomic percentages. XANES showed no Fe-Fe interaction, revealing single atomic Fe species. LCF fitting showed 72% Fe3O4 and 28% FeO for AuFeHS. EXAFS showed the first Fe peak at ~1.5Å, indicating non-elemental Fe. In-situ IR assigned 2105 cm-1 to Au0-CO and 2175 cm-1 to Auδ+-CO. Batch screening was carried out at 10 bar methane pressure. The reaction used H2O2 (15% w/v) as the oxidant. Continuous flow was performed in a fixed-bed reactor at atmospheric pressure. Gas chromatography and NMR confirmed product formation and quantification. CD4 isotope labeling confirmed the methyl group originated from methane. Nitrogen feed instead of methane resulted in no products.

Procedures And Architectures
The synthesis used NaOH-assisted deposition to incorporate Na into the silica matrix. FeHS formation decreased Q3 and Q2 states in solid-state NMR. Au deposition further decreased Q3 and Q2 states. Na 1s XPS confirmed the Si-O-Na interaction. 23Na NMR showed peaks at 7.32 ppm and -1.59 ppm for Si-O-Na framework. Pyridine-adsorbed FT-IR showed a band at 1449 cm-1 for Lewis acid sites. Pyridine-adsorbed FT-IR showed a band at ~1640 cm-1 for -OH deformation. The reaction proceeded via C-H sigma complex formation on acidic sites. The CH3 radical formed on low-valent Fe 3-δ+ sites. Au nanoparticles provided low-energy activation sites for CO adsorption. The control experiments showed no product without methane, oxidant, or catalyst. The continuous process showed steady methanol production over 7 h. The product yield reached a maximum at 4 h (157 µmol) under optimized conditions. Temperature optimization confirmed 80°C as the best condition. The reaction used a total gas pressure of 20 bar (15 bar CH4:5 bar CO) with CO co-feed.

Key Results
The support (HS) alone gave no product in the POM reaction. The Fe-HS catalyst gave 285 mmol/gFe with 82% methanol selectivity. The Au-HS catalyst gave only 47.6 mmol/gAu of methanol. The AuFeHS catalyst reached 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity in batch. Au and Fe on SBA-15 gave only 111 mmol/gFe+Au methanol. Fe-SBA-15 and Au-SBA-15 gave 0.30 and 0.15 mmol/gcat, respectively. The batch acetic acid yield was 3403 µmol/gcat within 1 h at 50°C. Methanol was the only other liquid oxygenate with 166 µmol/gcat yield. The CO2 selectivity was 10% with CO co-feed at 50°C. The continuous AuFeHS yield reached 224 mmol/gFe+Au. The continuous methanol productivity was 422 µmolh-1gcat-1 for 4 h. The continuous acetic acid yield was 648 µmol/gcat within 4 h. The AuFeHS yield surpassed the O2/O2H2O2 batch reports. The methanol yield exceeded the high-pressure H2O2 continuous report. The hydrophobic support enhanced activity versus SBA-15. The methanol selectivity was greater than 95% in batch.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The performance is attributed to the synergy between Fe and Au. Low-valent Fe 3-δ+ sites activate both CH4 and H2O2. Au stabilizes the low-valent Fe sites. The hydrophobicity and acidic sites are key for enhanced activity. The Lewis acid sites facilitate C-H sigma complex formation. The Au nanoparticles enable facile CO insertion and acetic acid generation. Tuning active Fe species through bimetallic modulation is a promising route. The work opens the scope for commercializing M2O technologies. The catalyst operates under benign atmospheric conditions.

Contradictions And Limitations
The role of Na and Lewis acid sites remains unexplored. The study explicitly states these aspects are beyond the scope. The exact reaction mechanism is not fully elucidated. The catalyst stability over long-term operation is not fully addressed.

Claims
The AuFeHS catalyst achieves high-yield, high-selectivity methane partial oxidation under benign conditions. The catalyst reached 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity in batch. The continuous yield reached 224 mmol/gFe+Au. The methanol selectivity was greater than 95%. The reaction operated at atmospheric pressure. The support alone gave no product. The monometallic catalysts gave much lower yields. The work supports commercialization of M2O technologies. The synergy between Au and Fe is a key design principle.
Co-feeding CO switches selectivity from methanol to acetic acid. The acetic acid yield was 648 µmol/gcat within 4 h. The selectivity switch produced acetic acid as the main product. The CO2 selectivity was 10% with CO co-feed. Methanol remained the only other liquid oxygenate. The catalyst enables access to acetic acid from methane. The CO insertion pathway is facilitated by Au sites.

Data And Code Availability
The supporting information is available free of charge via the Internet. The DOI is https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2023-h00ht. The license is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The control experiments showed no product without methane, oxidant, or catalyst. The isotope labeling confirmed the methyl group originated from methane. The nitrogen feed gave no products, ruling out background reactions. The hydrophobic support enhanced activity versus SBA-15. The monometallic catalysts gave much lower yields.

Ethical Considerations
The paper uses a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license. The content was not peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 shows HRTEM images of FeHS and AuFeHS catalysts. Fig. 2 shows XPS and XANES spectra of the catalysts. Fig. 3 shows catalytic activity and selectivity data. Fig. 4 shows continuous flow methanol production. Fig. 5 shows solid-state NMR of the silica support. Table S4 provides detailed comparison of catalytic activity. Table S6 compares with recent literature values.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is the AuFeHS catalyst for atmospheric-pressure methane oxidation. The strongest evidence is the 1666 mmol/gFe+Au yield with 95% selectivity. The future path is commercializing M2O technologies.
